questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. New review before go-live
questions.question: A risk analyst at a software company is helping the support manager set up a weekly review of bulk customer-data exports. What is MOST important to agree before the review goes live?

options.A: A documented procedure naming who performs the review
options.B: Internal audit's approval of the review design in advance
options.C: The risk owner's acceptance of a lower rating from the first review
options.D: The analyst's sign-off on the first review's results

questions.key_concept: A new control needs a documented procedure, a named performer and an evidence trail, agreed with the control owner before go-live.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the control needs in order to work from what the register will say once it does.
questions.correct_explanation: Before a control goes live, the analyst works with the support manager, as control owner, to document how the review is performed, who performs it and what evidence it leaves. Without that, the review cannot be tested and fails quietly when people change jobs. Recording a lower residual rating is premature: risk counts as reduced only after the review is shown to operate. The risk owner then accepts the new rating.

wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because audit gives assurance. Internal audit assesses controls independently afterward; approving management's design in advance would weaken that independence.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because the owner should accept the new rating. One review shows the control exists, not that it works; the rating changes once operation is shown.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because the analyst knows the risk. Signing off its results makes the analyst part of the control; the support team performs it and its manager answers for it.

tips: Eliminate: D makes the analyst part of the control by signing off its results, and B asks internal audit to approve a management control it must later assess independently.
Final two: A beats C because a control needs a documented procedure and a named performer before it can work; the residual rating changes only after it is shown to operate.
Exam cue: before go-live, look for a documented procedure, a named performer and an evidence trail; after go-live, look for proof it operates before lowering the risk.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Mixed rating scales
questions.question: An enterprise risk analyst at a retail group is combining unit risk registers: two units score risks from 1 to 5, and one uses high, medium and low. What should the analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Add each unit's scores together to rank the group's risks
options.B: Average the scores to weight each unit equally
options.C: Map the ratings onto one common scale and set of criteria
options.D: List each unit's top risks as rated in one combined table

questions.key_concept: Risk ratings from different scales must be normalized to common criteria before they are aggregated or compared.
questions.pre_read: Look at how each unit rates its risks before deciding how to combine them.
questions.correct_explanation: Ratings on different scales cannot be compared, added or averaged, so the first step is normalizing them onto the group's common scale and criteria, for example mapping high, medium and low to numbers. Only then can duplicates be merged and risks ranked across units. Listing each unit's top risks as rated keeps them visible, but leaves senior management comparing a 4 with a high.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because totals look decisive. Adding scores from different scales gives numbers with no shared meaning and can bury a severe single risk.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it seems fair to every unit. Averaging still mixes scales and pulls a critical risk toward the middle.
wrong_explanations.D: Tempting because nothing is lost. Without a common scale, readers cannot compare risks across units or rank them.

tips: Eliminate: A and B do arithmetic on ratings from different scales, which buries severe risks and gives totals with no common meaning.
Final two: C beats D because comparison needs common criteria first; a list kept on each unit's own scale keeps the risks visible but impossible to rank.
Exam cue: before aggregating risk data, normalize it; one scale and one set of criteria come before any ranking, totaling or reporting.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Unread alerts
questions.question: A law firm's monitoring tool sends alerts to a shared inbox when laptop antivirus is disabled, and the risk analyst finds the majority of them unread. What should the analyst recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Add a second monitoring tool to widen laptop coverage
options.B: Name an owner to check the shared inbox once a month
options.C: Flag the alerts as high priority in the shared inbox
options.D: Route each alert type to a responder with a deadline

questions.key_concept: Automated monitoring reduces risk only when each alert reaches a responder, named by role, who acts within a set time.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens after an alert is sent, and who is expected to act on it.
questions.correct_explanation: Monitoring reduces risk only when someone acts on what it finds. Alerts sent to a shared inbox have no owner, so disabled antivirus goes unanswered. Routing each alert type to a responder named by role, with a response deadline, tracked to closure, turns detection into response. A monthly inbox check names an owner but leaves laptops unprotected for weeks between checks, so it is the runner-up.

wrong_explanations.A: Tempting because broader coverage sounds safer. More alerts into an unread inbox add volume without adding any response.
wrong_explanations.B: Tempting because it names an owner. A monthly check leaves disabled antivirus unanswered for weeks; the response time must match how fast the exposure grows.
wrong_explanations.C: Tempting because urgent flags draw the eye. A flag gives no one the duty to act; alerts in an unowned inbox stay unread however they are marked.

tips: Eliminate: A adds alerts to a queue nobody works, and C makes unowned alerts louder without giving anyone the duty to act.
Final two: D beats B because each alert needs a responder, named by role, acting within a set time; a monthly inbox check names an owner but leaves exposure open for weeks.
Exam cue: when monitoring exists but nothing happens, the fix is ownership and a response time, not more alerts or louder ones.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Acceptance above delegated authority
questions.question: A logistics firm's policy lets department heads accept residual risks rated up to medium, and the warehouse head has signed acceptance of a residual risk rated high. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: File the signed acceptance in the register as approved
options.B: Refer the acceptance to the executive authorized for high risks
options.C: Lower the risk's rating to medium to match the signer's authority
options.D: Co-sign the acceptance on behalf of the risk function

questions.key_concept: Risk acceptance must come from someone whose delegated authority covers the rating; an acceptance beyond it is elevated.
questions.pre_read: Compare the rating the head may accept with the rating of this risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Acceptance authority is delegated by rating, so a high residual risk must be accepted by someone who holds that authority. The practitioner refers the decision upward, with the analysis, rather than filing an acceptance the signer could not give. Filing it is the closest alternative: the signature looks formal, but it records a decision outside policy and leaves the firm holding a high risk nobody with authority agreed to.

wrong_explanations.A: A signature outside delegated authority is not a valid acceptance. Filing it would record a high risk as approved when no one with that authority has agreed.
wrong_explanations.C: The rating comes from the analysis, not from who signed. Lowering it to fit the signer's authority would misstate the exposure.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk function advises and records; it does not accept risk. Its co-signature cannot supply authority the warehouse head lacks.

tips: Eliminate: C changes the analysis to suit the approver, and D has the risk function take part in an acceptance decision.
Final two: B beats A because an acceptance beyond the signer's delegated limit is not valid; it goes to the level that holds that authority.
Exam cue: when a decision exceeds someone's authority, elevate it to the level that holds the authority; never resize the risk to fit.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Worsening indicator below red
questions.question: An insurer's KCI tracks production changes deployed without an approved ticket. Over four months, the KCI rose from 2% to 9%, still below its 10% red threshold. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Wait until the KCI crosses its red threshold
options.B: Ask the control owner to raise the threshold to 15%
options.C: Review the rising trend with the control owner
options.D: Hand the control owner's approvals to the risk team

questions.key_concept: A worsening KCI trend is raised with the control owner before a threshold breach; the risk function challenges but does not run the control.
questions.pre_read: Look at the direction of the indicator, not only its distance from red.
questions.correct_explanation: A steady rise toward the threshold is a warning in its own right. The practitioner takes the trend to the control owner, who is accountable for change approval, to find the cause and fix it before the limit is breached. Waiting for the red threshold is the closest alternative: thresholds trigger escalation, but trend analysis exists so action can start before a breach.

wrong_explanations.A: Thresholds trigger escalation, but by the time this KCI turns red, more unapproved changes will have reached production.
wrong_explanations.B: Raising the threshold to fit current performance hides the decline and breaks the link between the threshold and tolerance.
wrong_explanations.D: The risk team oversees and challenges controls; taking over the owner's approvals would make it judge its own work and leave the owner's process unfixed.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the limit to fit the decline, and D has the second line run a first-line control.
Final two: C beats A because a worsening trend justifies action before the threshold; the control owner fixes the cause while there is still margin.
Exam cue: read indicators as trends; a steady move toward a threshold goes to the owner before it is breached.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. AI service outage
questions.question: A vendor's AI service failed for two days, halting a lender's mortgage approvals, and no trained staff remain to check documents by hand. Which of the following should the risk practitioner recommend as MOST important?

options.A: Higher service credits when the service is down
options.B: Spot checks of the documents the service has read
options.C: A stricter availability commitment in the vendor contract
options.D: A tested manual process for reading documents in outages

questions.key_concept: A contract can price an AI vendor's failure but cannot keep the business running; a high-risk AI service needs a tested fallback the enterprise controls.
questions.pre_read: Picture the next two-day failure and ask which option would keep approvals moving.
questions.correct_explanation: The failure exposed a dependency with no way around it: when the AI service stops, approvals stop. A tested manual or alternative process lets the lender keep approving loans during an outage, and only the lender can provide it. A stricter availability commitment may reduce how often the vendor fails and adds remedies, but when it does fail, approvals still halt and customers still hold the lender accountable.

wrong_explanations.A: Service credits refund part of the fees after an outage; they do nothing to keep mortgage approvals moving while the service is down.
wrong_explanations.B: Sampling checks the accuracy of what the service reads, a different risk from the outage that halted approvals.
wrong_explanations.C: A stronger commitment adds remedies and may improve uptime, but approvals still stop the next time the service fails.

tips: Eliminate: A refunds fees without keeping the business running, and B checks output accuracy when the risk shown is the service being unavailable.
Final two: D beats C because a contract term cannot keep approvals moving when the vendor fails; a tested fallback the lender controls can.
Exam cue: for a high-risk third-party AI service, look for a contingency the business controls; contracts move cost, not accountability or continuity.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Tool proposed to replace a policy
questions.question: An engineering consultancy's IT director proposes retiring the data handling policy and staff training because the new data-loss prevention tool now blocks unsafe file sharing. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: Retire the policy and record the tool as the control
options.B: Replace the training with pop-up warnings from the tool
options.C: Test the tool's blocking before retiring the policy
options.D: Keep the policy and training alongside the tool

questions.key_concept: Technical controls depend on administrative ones: the policy sets what is sensitive and who is accountable, and training covers what the tool cannot see.
questions.pre_read: Ask what tells the tool which files to block, and who answers when it gets one wrong.
questions.correct_explanation: Control categories work together. The policy defines what data is sensitive, how it may be shared and who is accountable; the tool's rules are written from it, and training covers handling the tool cannot see, such as printed or spoken data. Testing the tool's blocking first sounds prudent, but even a tool that works perfectly needs the policy and training behind it, so a good test result would not justify retiring them.

wrong_explanations.A: A technical control is not stronger by default; without the policy, the tool's rules have no agreed basis and no one owns the choices they encode.
wrong_explanations.B: Pop-up warnings reach people only at the moment of sharing; they do not teach the handling rules that apply where the tool cannot see.
wrong_explanations.C: Testing confirms the tool blocks what it is set to block, but a passing test does not remove the need for the policy that sets the rules.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a technical control as stronger by default, and B replaces training with warnings that only appear where the tool can see.
Final two: D beats C because the policy is what the tool's rules are built on and training covers what the tool cannot see; even a good test result would not justify retiring them.
Exam cue: a gap in one control category is not filled by strength in another; prefer the option that keeps the control the others depend on.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Plan complete but short of target
questions.question: All actions in a retailer's risk action plan are complete and tested as working. The re-rated risk is within appetite but above the target risk the plan set. What is the risk practitioner's BEST action?

options.A: Close the plan and record the risk as within appetite
options.B: Lower the plan's target risk to match the new rating
options.C: Take the shortfall to the risk owner for a decision
options.D: Ask the action owners to add a further control

questions.key_concept: A plan is judged against its own target; if risk ends above it, even within appetite, the risk owner decides whether to accept the gap.
questions.pre_read: Separate whether the actions were done from whether the plan achieved what it promised.
questions.correct_explanation: The plan delivered its actions, but its purpose was to bring the risk to the target the owner set. Within appetite the gap could be accepted, but that is the risk owner's decision, so the practitioner reports the shortfall with the validated rating. Closing the plan because the risk is within appetite is the runner-up: acceptance may be right, but it is the owner's call, not an automatic close.

wrong_explanations.A: Being within appetite makes acceptance possible, but the plan promised a lower target; closing it without the owner's decision skips the person who set that target.
wrong_explanations.B: Moving the target to fit the result reverses the logic; the target was set with the risk owner within appetite, not from what the plan happened to achieve.
wrong_explanations.D: More control may be the answer, but deciding further treatment belongs to the risk owner; action owners carry out the tasks they are given.

tips: Eliminate: B moves the target to fit the result, and D has action owners choose treatment that is the risk owner's call.
Final two: C beats A because the owner set the target; being within appetite makes acceptance possible, but the owner decides whether to accept the gap.
Exam cue: a plan is judged against its own target; when it falls short, even within appetite, the risk owner decides what happens next.

questions.subtopic: 3C4 Risk and control monitoring techniques. Ending scheduled reviews
questions.question: An airport operator now starts a risk reassessment on every major change, incident and threshold breach, and its CIO proposes ending scheduled risk reviews. What is the risk practitioner's BEST response?

options.A: End the scheduled reviews and rely on the triggers
options.B: Replace scheduled reviews with a KRI summary report
options.C: Keep scheduled reviews alongside the triggers
options.D: Keep scheduled reviews for the ten highest risks

questions.key_concept: Triggers catch change that someone records; scheduled reviews stay as a backstop for change nobody reports, at a frequency set by risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a trigger depends on to fire, and what happens when that does not occur.
questions.correct_explanation: Triggers fire only when someone records a change, incident or breach; drift, unreported changes and slow shifts in threats pass them by. Scheduled reviews remain the backstop, with frequency set by each risk's rating. Keeping them for the ten highest risks saves effort, but it leaves every other risk without a backstop, even though an unreported change can turn a low-rated risk into a serious one.

wrong_explanations.A: Triggers depend on someone recording the event; without scheduled reviews, unreported change and gradual drift are never picked up.
wrong_explanations.B: A KRI summary shows indicator movement, but risks without KRIs, and changes no indicator tracks, would go unreviewed.
wrong_explanations.D: Limiting reviews to the top ten leaves lower-rated risks with no backstop, though unreported change can raise them.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes triggers catch every change, and B assumes indicators cover every risk.
Final two: C beats D because unreported change can affect any risk; keep a backstop for all of them, with frequency set by rating.
Exam cue: event triggers and scheduled reviews work together; an option that drops either one is the trap.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. Comparing the options
questions.question: Which of the following BEST helps a risk owner choose among the response options a risk practitioner has identified for a risk above appetite?

options.A: The control the IT team prefers for the risk
options.B: The responses peer firms chose for similar risks
options.C: The risk's inherent rating before controls
options.D: Each alternative's cost and the target risk it leaves

questions.key_concept: The practitioner sets out each response option with its cost and the target risk it would leave; the risk owner chooses.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a decision-maker needs in order to compare options against appetite.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk owner decides by comparing what each option costs with where it would leave the risk against appetite, so the practitioner sets out each option's cost and target risk side by side. Peer firms' choices are the runner-up: they show what others did, but those firms have their own appetite, costs and exposure, so they cannot tell this owner which option fits.

wrong_explanations.A: IT's preferred control is one option, not a comparison; it skips what each option costs and the risk each would leave.
wrong_explanations.B: Peers' choices reflect their own appetite, costs and exposure, so they cannot show which option fits this organization.
wrong_explanations.C: The inherent rating is the same starting point for every option, so it cannot separate one response from another.

tips: Eliminate: A narrows the choice to IT's favorite control, and C gives a rating that is the same whichever option is chosen.
Final two: D beats B because the owner needs this organization's costs and resulting risk; peers chose for their own appetite.
Exam cue: the practitioner lays out options with cost and target risk; the owner picks the one that meets appetite at a fair price.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Does the KRI warn?
questions.question: A bank's risk committee asks whether its two-year-old KRI for failed sign-in attempts actually warns of account takeovers. Which of the following analyses should the risk analyst use to BEST answer?

options.A: Compare the KRI's level with other banks' figures
options.B: Line up past KRI rises with incident dates
options.C: Reconcile the KRI's data with the sign-in logs
options.D: Poll the KRI's users on its usefulness

questions.key_concept: A KRI's predictive value is tested against its history: a leading KRI moves before the incidents it is meant to warn of.
questions.pre_read: Pin down exactly what the committee is asking about the KRI.
questions.correct_explanation: A KRI warns only if it moves before the event. Checking two years of values against when account takeovers happened shows whether rises in failed sign-ins came first, which is the committee's question. Reconciling the data with the sign-in logs is the runner-up: it confirms the figures are accurate, but an accurate figure can still fail to predict anything.

wrong_explanations.A: Other banks' figures show whether the level is high or low, not whether this KRI moves before takeovers at this bank.
wrong_explanations.C: Reconciling to the logs checks accuracy, which matters, but accurate data says nothing about whether the KRI rises before takeovers.
wrong_explanations.D: Users' views show whether the KRI is liked or used, not whether its values have predicted takeovers.

tips: Eliminate: A compares levels with other banks, and D collects opinions; neither tests whether the KRI warns.
Final two: B beats C because the question is predictive power; accurate data can still describe a KRI that never warns.
Exam cue: to test whether a KRI leads, line its history up against past incidents and see which moved first.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Signal heard first by staff
questions.question: A water utility's horizon scan of news and alert feeds caught scam texts using its name after a press story. Call-center staff had heard of them for months. What is the risk practitioner's BEST recommendation?

options.A: Add a second commercial news-monitoring service
options.B: Feed front-line teams' reports into the scan
options.C: Move the horizon scan to a weekly schedule
options.D: Record scam risks once customers report a loss

questions.key_concept: Horizon scanning should draw on front-line teams as well as external feeds, since staff often see an emerging risk first.
questions.pre_read: Note each source that could have picked up the scam texts.
questions.correct_explanation: The signal existed inside the utility for months: call-center staff were hearing about the scam texts. A scan built only on external feeds misses what front-line teams see first, so their reports should feed it. A second news service is the runner-up: it widens the external view, but it would still have waited for the same press story.

wrong_explanations.A: Another news service adds more of the same external sources, which reported the scam only once the press had it.
wrong_explanations.C: Scanning more often does not help when the sources themselves lag; the internal signal would still be missed.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting for a reported loss is the trap; emerging risks are recorded and watched before they cause harm.

tips: Eliminate: C repeats the same lagging sources more often, and D waits for a loss before recording the risk.
Final two: B beats A because the missed signal came from inside the utility; more external feeds would still lag.
Exam cue: horizon scanning draws on front-line staff as well as external feeds; insiders often see a new risk first.

questions.subtopic: 3C6 Monitoring and reporting of emerging risks. Reviews that find nothing
questions.question: A vacation-rental platform has an emerging risk of AI-generated fake listings. Each six-monthly review asks the owner only whether anything changed. The last three answers were no. What should the risk practitioner recommend as BEST?

options.A: Agree with the owner to review the entry each quarter
options.B: Rate the risk on the usual scale in the main profile
options.C: Close the entry until the first AI-made fake listing is found
options.D: Agree with the owner on signs that the risk is growing

questions.key_concept: Emerging risks are watched through agreed signs that would show them growing, so each review checks evidence rather than asking if anything changed.
questions.pre_read: Note what each review actually asks the owner.
questions.correct_explanation: The reviews keep finding nothing because they ask only whether anything has changed, with nothing named to check. Agreeing signs that would show the risk growing, such as reported fake listings or cheaper tools for faking photos, gives each review evidence to weigh and tells the owner when to act. A shorter cycle is the runner-up: asking the same open question more often still finds nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Reviewing more often repeats the same open question; with nothing named to check, a three-month review finds nothing new either.
wrong_explanations.B: Nothing new is known, so a usual rating would claim certainty the evidence lacks; an emerging risk joins the main profile once it can be rated with confidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Waiting for the first case records the risk only after it has caused harm, which an emerging-risk entry exists to avoid.

tips: Eliminate: B rates the risk with confidence nobody has, and C waits for the first case, losing the early warning the entry is for.
Final two: D beats A because the reviews ask an open question with nothing named to check; asking it more often still finds nothing.
Exam cue: an emerging risk needs named signs to watch, so each review has evidence to check and the owner knows when to act.

questions.subtopic: 3A3 Vendor/supply chain risk management. Supplier risk terms
questions.question: A risk practitioner is explaining supplier risks to a university's new procurement head. Which of the following BEST describes concentration risk?

options.A: One supplier's controls failing its latest security review
options.B: A supplier passing customer data on to its subcontractors
options.C: Reliance on a few suppliers whose failure stops many services
options.D: The cost and effort of moving off a supplier's platform

questions.key_concept: Concentration risk is reliance on a few suppliers whose failure would stop many services at once, judged across suppliers rather than one at a time.
questions.pre_read: Note what each option measures before matching it to the term.
questions.correct_explanation: The ISACA Glossary describes concentration risk as reliance on a small number of suppliers, so one supplier's failure can stop every service built on it. It is judged across suppliers, by what depends on each, not one supplier at a time. Lock-in is the runner-up: it also comes from depending on a supplier, but it is the cost of leaving one, not the harm when one fails.

wrong_explanations.A: A failed review is one supplier's control weakness, rated on its own; concentration is about how many services depend on the same few suppliers.
wrong_explanations.B: Onward sharing with subcontractors is a fourth-party data risk; it concerns where data goes, not how many services stop if one supplier fails.
wrong_explanations.D: Lock-in is the cost and effort of leaving a supplier; it can deepen dependence, but it measures the exit, not the services a failure would stop.

tips: Eliminate: A rates one supplier's own controls, and B is about data passing to subcontractors; neither shows how much depends on a few suppliers.
Final two: C beats D because concentration is the harm when a relied-on supplier fails; lock-in is the cost of leaving one.
Exam cue: concentration risk is judged across suppliers by what depends on each; one supplier's score or exit cost does not show it.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for an AI screening tool
questions.question: Which of the following should the risk analyst propose as the BEST key risk indicator that a recruitment agency's AI CV-screening tool is unfairly rejecting candidates?

options.A: Upheld discrimination complaints from rejected candidates
options.B: Monthly gap in pass rates between candidate groups
options.C: Screening accuracy reported by the tool's vendor
options.D: Share of CVs screened within an hour of arrival

questions.key_concept: A KRI for unfair AI decisions compares outcomes across groups on the organization's own data; overall accuracy can hide the gap.
questions.pre_read: Ask how the named harm would first show up in the data, then match each measure to it.
questions.correct_explanation: Unfair rejection first shows as a gap between groups' pass rates, so tracking that gap monthly warns while the agency can still correct the tool, before complaints or regulators act. The vendor's reported accuracy is the runner-up: it sounds like the model's own risk measure, but overall accuracy can stay high while one group is rejected far more often, and it reflects the vendor's tests, not the agency's candidates.

wrong_explanations.A: Upheld complaints count harm already done and confirmed months later; this lagging measure explains a loss rather than warning of one.
wrong_explanations.C: Overall accuracy can stay high while one group is rejected far more often, and the vendor's figure comes from its own tests, not these candidates.
wrong_explanations.D: Screening speed is a performance measure for the process; it can look excellent while the tool rejects some groups unfairly.

tips: Eliminate: A counts complaints upheld after the harm, a lagging measure, and D measures screening speed, a KPI that need not move with fairness.
Final two: B beats C because unfair rejection shows as a gap between groups; one overall accuracy figure from the vendor's tests can hide it.
Exam cue: for AI fairness risk, pick an indicator that compares outcomes across groups on your own data, not one overall accuracy figure.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. Finding whose risk is within appetite
questions.question: An audit found contractors reach a housing association's repairs system without multifactor sign-in. The analyzed risk is within appetite. The risk owner would accept it rather than fund a $90,000 fix. What is the risk analyst's BEST advice?

options.A: Let the finding close on the risk owner's recorded acceptance
options.B: Get internal audit's approval for the owner's decision
options.C: Fund the quoted $90,000 multifactor fix for contractor sign-in
options.D: Have the system's IT owner sign the risk acceptance

questions.key_concept: An audit finding can close on a recorded risk acceptance when the analyzed risk is within appetite; the risk owner decides, not internal audit.
questions.pre_read: Compare the finding's analyzed risk with appetite before deciding how it closes.
questions.correct_explanation: An audit finding reports a gap; it does not oblige a fix. The analyzed risk is within appetite, so its owner may accept it, and recording that acceptance against the finding lets the finding close on a documented decision that internal audit can follow up. Fixing the gap for $90,000 is the runner-up: it also closes the finding, but spends money on a risk already within appetite.

wrong_explanations.B: Internal audit reports and follows up findings independently; approving management's risk decisions would compromise that independence, and the decision belongs to the risk owner.
wrong_explanations.C: Fixing closes the finding, but spends $90,000 on a risk already within appetite; a finding can also close on the owner's recorded acceptance.
wrong_explanations.D: The IT owner runs the repairs system but does not own the business risk; acceptance comes from the risk owner, who answers for the loss.

tips: Eliminate: B asks internal audit to approve a management decision, compromising its independence, and D has the system's IT owner accept a business risk.
Final two: A beats C because the risk is within appetite; an audit finding can close on a recorded acceptance rather than a $90,000 fix.
Exam cue: an audit finding is not an order to fix; when the analyzed risk is within appetite, the risk owner may accept it on record.

questions.subtopic: 3C1 Risk action plans. Plans tracked in a project tool
questions.question: A tram operator tracks risk action plans only in a project tool, and five finished in March, yet its risk register still lists them as under way. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Have action owners email the risk team as each action closes
options.B: Have action owners log progress in each register entry
options.C: Re-rate the five risks in the register from the project tool
options.D: Ask risk owners to track their plans in the project tool

questions.key_concept: Each action plan is tied to its risk's register entry, so progress, slippage and closure reach the risk picture that reports draw on.
questions.pre_read: Ask where the picture of each risk lives, and whether plan progress ever reaches it.
questions.correct_explanation: The register holds the risk picture, but the plans live only in the project tool, so finished work never reaches it. Having action owners log progress in each risk's register entry keeps plan and risk in one view, ready for the risk team to validate the work and re-rate. Closure emails are the runner-up: they cover the finish line only, leave milestones and slippage outside the register, and depend on someone remembering.

wrong_explanations.A: Closure emails cover only the finish; milestones and slippage stay outside the register, and a forgotten email recreates the gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Re-rating from the project tool's status credits work nobody has validated; finished actions are tested before a risk's rating changes.
wrong_explanations.D: Moving risk owners into the project tool deepens the split; the register still would not show plan progress.

tips: Eliminate: C re-rates on unvalidated tool status, and D pulls risk owners further into a tool the register never sees.
Final two: B beats A because logging progress in the register entry carries milestones and slippage too; closure emails cover only the finish and depend on memory.
Exam cue: an action plan belongs with its risk's register entry, so progress and closure update the risk picture; ratings change only after validation.

questions.subtopic: 3A1 Risk response options. A control that serves several risks
questions.question: Which of the following BEST shows an open university's risk analyst the benefit of a control reducing five risks, to weigh against its cost?

options.A: Reduction in each of the five risks' ratings
options.B: Expected loss avoided on the highest-rated of the five risks
options.C: Expected loss avoided, summed across the five risks
options.D: Spending on the same control at peer universities

questions.key_concept: A control's benefit is the expected loss it avoids across every risk it reduces, weighed against its full cost.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a control's benefit is made of before comparing the measures offered.
questions.correct_explanation: A control's benefit is the loss it is expected to avoid, so when one control reduces five risks, its benefit is the reduction summed across all five, weighed against its full cost. The loss avoided on the highest-rated risk is the runner-up: it is only part of the benefit, so judging the control on it understates the case and can reject a control that pays for itself across the five.

wrong_explanations.A: Rating drops show each risk moving, but not a value that can be summed or weighed against the control's cost.
wrong_explanations.B: The highest-rated risk shows only part of the benefit; leaving out the other four understates the control's value and can reject a sound investment.
wrong_explanations.D: Peer spending is a cost benchmark, showing what others paid; it says nothing about the loss this control would avoid at the university.

tips: Eliminate: A shows rating changes with no value to weigh against cost, and D counts peers' spending; neither measures the loss the control would avoid.
Final two: C beats B because a control's benefit is all the loss it avoids; scoring it on one risk understates the case.
Exam cue: in a cost-benefit case, count the risk reduction across every risk a control serves, then weigh it against the control's full cost.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Tailoring COBIT 2019
questions.question: A regional blood service's risk analyst is helping tailor COBIT 2019 to the service. Which of the following is the PRIMARY input COBIT 2019 uses to set which objectives get priority?

options.A: Capability levels assessed for each current process
options.B: Baselines chosen from each system's impact level
options.C: Design factors such as strategy and threat landscape
options.D: CSF Tiers matched to current risk practices

questions.key_concept: COBIT 2019 is tailored through design factors, such as enterprise strategy and the threat landscape, which set objective priorities and target capability levels.
questions.pre_read: Place each option in the framework it comes from, then ask which one describes the enterprise itself.
questions.correct_explanation: COBIT 2019 is generic, so each enterprise tailors it: design factors describing its context, such as strategy, size, regulation and the threat landscape, set which of the 40 objectives get priority and what capability each should reach. Assessing current capability is the runner-up: COBIT uses it to measure how well processes perform and to find gaps once targets are set, but it does not decide which objectives matter.

wrong_explanations.A: Capability assessment measures how well processes perform today; it shows gaps against targets once priorities are set, not which objectives matter to this service.
wrong_explanations.B: Impact-level baselines come from NIST SP 800-53B, for selecting each system's security controls; they are not how COBIT is tailored.
wrong_explanations.D: Tiers belong to NIST CSF 2.0 and describe the rigor of cybersecurity risk practices; COBIT 2019 does not use them to tailor its objectives.

tips: Eliminate: B and D come from other frameworks: impact-level baselines are NIST SP 800-53B, and Tiers are NIST CSF 2.0.
Final two: C beats A because capability levels measure how well processes run; design factors describe the enterprise, and that context sets which objectives get priority.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Indicator for an AI voice agent
questions.question: A call center outsourcer's AI voice agent can give callers wrong answers. Operations propose a KRI: the share of calls the agent closes without a human. Which KRI should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Share of agent-handled issues raised a second time
options.B: Share of calls the agent closes without a human
options.C: Error rate found in the vendor's pre-launch tests
options.D: Number of complaints clients escalate about the agent

questions.key_concept: A KRI for an AI agent's wrong answers tracks an early live sign, such as issues raised a second time, not efficiency or complaints.
questions.pre_read: For each measure, ask whether it would move before clients feel the harm, and whether it tracks wrong answers at all.
questions.correct_explanation: A KRI should move before the harm lands. A caller who raises the same issue again is an early sign that the agent's answer failed, visible before complaints or client penalties, and it comes from the outsourcer's own call records. Escalated complaints are the runner-up: they relate directly to wrong answers, but they lag, arriving after clients are already unhappy, and many callers given a wrong answer never complain.

wrong_explanations.B: Closing calls without a human is a performance measure; it can rise while the agent keeps callers it answers wrongly, so it does not warn of the risk.
wrong_explanations.C: A pre-launch error rate is one past figure from the vendor's tests; it cannot show how the agent is answering live calls now.
wrong_explanations.D: Escalated complaints show real harm but arrive late, after clients are unhappy, and many callers given a wrong answer never complain.

tips: Eliminate: B is a performance measure that can rise while wrong answers grow, and C is a one-off vendor figure from before launch, not live monitoring.
Final two: A beats D because callers raise a failed answer again soon after, while escalated complaints arrive after the harm, and only some callers complain.
Exam cue: for an AI agent's error risk, prefer a live signal in your own records that moves before harm builds, over efficiency rates, vendor test scores or complaint counts.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. Credited review nobody runs
questions.question: A pallet maker's rating of its kiln-tampering risk credits a remote-access review. The review's named owner, the IT manager, never knew of it, and no review has run. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Confirm the IT manager as the review's control owner
options.B: Run the review within the risk team until one is named
options.C: Remove the review and its owner from the register
options.D: Report to the risk owner that the review never ran

questions.key_concept: A credited control that never ran leaves current risk above its rating; the owner of that risk hears first, before the control's ownership is fixed.
questions.pre_read: Separate what the register says from what has actually happened, and ask who relied on the difference.
questions.correct_explanation: The kiln risk's rating counts a review that has never operated, so today's exposure is higher than the rating shows. The risk owner relies on that rating and must decide the interim response and see that the review gets a willing owner. Confirming the IT manager is the runner-up: an owner who never knew of the control cannot simply be confirmed, and the risk owner would still not know the rating was wrong.

wrong_explanations.A: The review does need an owner, but naming someone who never agreed fixes the record, not the gap, and the risk owner still does not know the rating is overstated.
wrong_explanations.B: The risk team oversees and challenges controls; running a first-line review would leave it checking its own work and still unowned by the business.
wrong_explanations.C: Deleting the entry hides that a credited control never ran; the risk it was meant to reduce is unchanged and the risk's owner is still unaware.

tips: Eliminate: B has the risk team run a first-line control, which is not its role, and C deletes the record of a credited control while the exposure it was meant to cut stays.
Final two: D beats A because the risk owner relies on a rating that counts this review; they must learn it never ran before the owner gap is filled.
Exam cue: when validation finds a credited control that never ran, the owner of the risk it protects learns the rating is overstated before anyone settles who owns the control.

questions.subtopic: 3A4 Issues, findings, exceptions and exemptions management. AI coding errors closed one by one
questions.question: A market research firm's issues log holds 14 cases of its AI tool miscoding open survey answers. Each case was closed once analysts fixed that client's report. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Track them as one finding with its cause and an agreed plan
options.B: Escalate the 14 cases to the AI vendor's account owner
options.C: Close each new case once the report's owner signs it off
options.D: Stop using the AI tool to code open survey answers

questions.key_concept: Repeated issues closed one at a time hide their cause; one finding for them lets the cause be analyzed and fixed under an agreed plan.
questions.pre_read: Look at how the log has closed these cases so far, and ask what that way of closing them cannot show.
questions.correct_explanation: Fourteen miscodings closed one at a time hide a pattern: each fix repairs one report while the cause stays. One finding lets the firm analyze why the tool miscodes and agree a plan with the tool's owner, tracked to validated closure. Escalating to the vendor is the runner-up: the vendor may help, but the cause is not yet known and may lie in the firm's own coding frames.

wrong_explanations.B: The vendor may be part of the fix, but sending it the cases before the cause is known skips the firm's own analysis, owner and plan.
wrong_explanations.C: An owner's sign-off is a statement, not evidence, and closing each case on its own keeps hiding the repeated pattern and its cause.
wrong_explanations.D: Dropping the tool gives up its benefit before anyone knows why it miscodes; the cause may be fixable at modest cost.

tips: Eliminate: C closes each case on an owner's sign-off, a statement rather than evidence, and D drops the tool before anyone knows why it miscodes.
Final two: A beats B because repeats of one issue become one finding, with the cause analyzed and an agreed plan; escalating to the vendor picks a fix before the cause is known.
Exam cue: when the same issue keeps being logged and closed, look for the option that treats the repeats as one problem with a cause, an owner and a plan, not another one-off fix.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. High pass rate, top risk exposed
questions.question: A microfinance lender's risk committee report says 94% of tested controls passed. The failures include both controls over the lender's top-rated risk, mobile loan fraud. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST change?

options.A: Report the pass rate for each business unit too
options.B: List each failed control with its owner and fix date
options.C: Show the failures against the risks they leave exposed
options.D: Exclude failed controls that their owners are already fixing

questions.key_concept: Control test results are reported against the risks they protect, so a high overall pass rate cannot hide failures behind a top risk.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the committee can decide from a pass rate, and what that figure cannot show it.
questions.correct_explanation: A 94% pass rate tells the committee little when the failures sit on the controls behind its top risk. Showing failures against the risks they leave exposed lets members see that mobile loan fraud has lost both its controls and decide what to do. Listing each failure with its owner and fix date is the runner-up: owners need that action list, but it does not show the committee which risks are exposed.

wrong_explanations.A: Splitting the pass rate by unit still averages over controls; the two failures behind the top risk stay hidden in the figures.
wrong_explanations.B: Owners need the action list, but the committee decides on risk; a list of failed controls does not show which risks lost protection.
wrong_explanations.D: Failures being fixed still leave their risks exposed until the fixes work; dropping them hides the top risk's lost controls from the committee.

tips: Eliminate: A is still an aggregate rate across many controls, split by unit, and D drops failures already being fixed, hiding exposure that stays until the fixes work.
Final two: C beats B because the committee needs failures shown by the risks they expose; an owner-and-date list suits the owners managing the fixes.
Exam cue: an overall pass rate averages away failures that cluster on one risk; set results against the risks they protect so a concentrated gap stands out.

questions.subtopic: 3C3 Risk and control metrics. Admin-rights indicator as staff grow
questions.question: A data center's KRI for admin-rights misuse is the share of accounts with admin rights. It fell from 4% to 3% while admin accounts rose from 20 to 30. Which KRI should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Number of accounts holding admin rights
options.B: Share of accounts with admin rights, shown by site
options.C: Breaches traced to misused admin rights
options.D: Admin-rights requests approved by system owners

questions.key_concept: When each item is its own path to harm, count the items; a share of a growing base can fall while the exposure rises.
questions.pre_read: Work out whether the risk grows with the number of items or with their share of a total.
questions.correct_explanation: Each admin account is a path to misuse, so exposure grows with how many there are, not with their share of all accounts. Here the share fell only because staff numbers grew, while admin accounts rose by half; a count shows that rise. The share by site is the runner-up: it adds detail, but each site's figure still shrinks as headcount grows, even while admin accounts multiply.

wrong_explanations.B: Splitting the share by site still divides admin accounts by headcount, so staff growth keeps hiding growth in admin rights.
wrong_explanations.C: Breaches are counted after misuse has happened; a KRI should warn while the exposure is building.
wrong_explanations.D: Approvals measure how busy the request process is, not how many admin accounts exist or whether they are still needed.

tips: Eliminate: C counts breaches after the misuse, a lagging measure, and D counts approvals, an activity of the request process rather than the exposure.
Final two: A beats B because exposure here grows with each admin account; a share divided by headcount falls as staff grow, even while admin accounts multiply.

questions.subtopic: 3B1 Control frameworks, types and standards. Automatic rollback of an AI pricing model
questions.question: A perfume retailer's AI pricing service reverts automatically to the last approved model version when a release's price errors exceed their limit. Which of the following is the risk analyst's BEST classification of this rollback?

options.A: A preventive control that stops a faulty release going live
options.B: A corrective control that restores a known good version
options.C: A detective control that finds a release's price errors
options.D: A compensating control that stands in for release testing

questions.key_concept: A control that restores a known good state after a fault is corrective; the check that spots the fault is the detective part.
questions.pre_read: Ask when the rollback acts: before the release, as errors are found, or after.
questions.correct_explanation: A corrective control fixes errors once they are detected. The rollback acts after a faulty release is live, restoring the last approved version so wrong prices stop spreading; the error limit that triggers it is the detective part. Detective is the runner-up: the rollback depends on that check, but finding the errors is not what the rollback itself does; it acts on what the check found.

wrong_explanations.A: The faulty release is already live when the rollback fires, so it cannot stop the release going out; testing before release would be preventive.
wrong_explanations.C: The error limit check detects the fault, but the rollback is the step that acts on it; each part is classified by what it does.
wrong_explanations.D: A compensating control stands in for a missing or weak control; the rollback adds recovery and replaces nothing.

tips: Eliminate: A acts after the release is live, so it cannot stop it going out, and D replaces no missing control, so it does not compensate.
Final two: B beats C because the rollback restores the approved version after the fault; the limit check that triggers it is the detective part.
Exam cue: when an AI or automated service reverts itself to a known good version after a fault, the reversal is corrective; the check that triggers it detects.

questions.subtopic: 3C2 Data collection, aggregation, analysis and validation. Branch counts to different cut-offs
questions.question: A locksmith firm's monthly KRI for lost master keys adds branch figures. Three of 12 branches report counts to the 15th, when their old system closes its month. What should the risk analyst do FIRST?

options.A: Exclude the three branches from the KRI total
options.B: Ask the three branches for counts to the month-end cut-off
options.C: Have the risk owner agree to add the branches' counts as reported
options.D: Show the KRI as the share of branches reporting a loss

questions.key_concept: Figures added into one KRI must cover the same period; a cut-off mismatch that can be fixed at source is fixed before adding them.
questions.pre_read: Check whether every branch's count covers the same days before they are added.
questions.correct_explanation: Counts to the 15th cover different days from the rest, so the total mixes two periods and misstates the month. Asking the three branches for counts to the month-end cut-off comes first, as the figure may be fixable at source. Having the risk owner agree to the counts as reported is the runner-up: each still covers a month, and steady offsets are sometimes tolerated, but late-month losses would land in the next report.

wrong_explanations.A: Leaving out three branches makes the total incomplete, and keys lost there would vanish from the KRI instead of being counted.
wrong_explanations.C: A steady offset is sometimes tolerated, but agreeing to it leaves losses after the 15th in next month's figure; nobody has yet asked whether these branches can count to month-end.
wrong_explanations.D: A share of branches with a loss still mixes counts from different periods and hides how many keys were lost; it changes the measure, not the data.

tips: Eliminate: A drops three branches from the KRI, and D changes the measure while still mixing counts from different periods.
Final two: B beats C because nobody has yet asked whether the branches can count to month-end; agreeing to the offset leaves their losses after the 15th in next month's KRI.
Exam cue: when sources feeding one KRI close their periods on different dates, get figures to one common cut-off before adding; a stated mismatch is for sources that cannot be fixed in time.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Repair invoices outside the match
questions.question: A shopping center landlord's system pays invoices only once they match a purchase order. But emergency repair invoices, a quarter of spend, bypass the system unchecked. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Budget owner approval of emergency invoices ahead of payment
options.B: A later review of paid emergency invoices against repair records
options.C: Reporting of spend paid outside the match to budget owners
options.D: Sign-off of emergency invoices by the contractor's own supervisor

questions.key_concept: A control covers only the transactions that pass through it; a route around it, such as emergency payments, needs its own check before the loss.
questions.pre_read: Trace which transactions pass through the control and which do not.
questions.correct_explanation: A control protects only what passes through it, so control analysis follows every route around it. A quarter of spend skips the match, so that route needs a check of its own. Approval by the budget owner before each emergency invoice is paid stops wrong payments without slowing urgent repairs. A later review against repair records is the runner-up: it finds false or duplicate invoices only after the money has gone.

wrong_explanations.B: A later review is detective: it finds false or duplicate repair invoices after payment, when recovering money is harder, while an approval before payment stops them.
wrong_explanations.C: Measuring the spend outside the match shows how big the gap is, but it puts no check on the invoices paid outside it.
wrong_explanations.D: The contractor's supervisor works for the firm being paid; a party approving its own invoices cannot show whether the charges are genuine.

tips: Eliminate: C measures the unchecked spend without checking any of it, and D lets the firm being paid approve its own invoices, which segregation of duties rules out.
Final two: A beats B because a quarter of spend leaves with no check; an approval before payment stops a bad invoice, while a later review finds it once the money is gone.
Exam cue: when analyzing a control, look for routes around it; a route that skips the check needs its own control, placed before the loss where it can be.

questions.subtopic: 3A2 Risk and control ownership. A risk re-rated beyond its owner's authority
questions.question: A nut processor's plant manager owns its allergen-labeling risk and can accept risks up to medium. After a five-year supermarket contract tripled volume, the risk is re-rated critical. What should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: Keep the plant manager as owner, referring each decision upward
options.B: Re-rate the risk as medium, counting planned label checks
options.C: Give the risk committee the risk to hold as a group
options.D: Move the risk to an executive with authority for its rating

questions.key_concept: A risk owner needs authority that matches the risk's rating; when a lasting re-rating exceeds it, ownership moves up to someone who can decide.
questions.pre_read: Compare the owner's authority with the risk's new rating.
questions.correct_explanation: Ownership should match a risk's rating: the owner funds the response and accepts what remains. The five-year contract makes the critical rating lasting and beyond the plant manager's authority, so moving the risk to an executive with authority for that rating puts the decisions with someone who can make them. Keeping the plant manager as owner and referring each decision upward is the runner-up: it leaves an owner who can decide nothing.

wrong_explanations.A: Referring a decision upward suits a one-off acceptance; with a lasting critical rating, it leaves a named owner who can neither accept the risk nor fund its response.
wrong_explanations.B: Planned checks give a target, not the current rating; re-rating on them to fit the owner's limit shrinks the risk to suit the authority.
wrong_explanations.C: A committee can oversee and challenge, but a risk held by a group often means no one acts; one named executive should own it.

tips: Eliminate: B rates the risk on planned checks to fit the owner's limit, and C hands it to a committee, where shared holding leaves no one accountable.
Final two: D beats A because the five-year contract keeps the rating critical; an owner who must refer every decision upward holds the title while the executive above makes the decisions.
Exam cue: when a risk's rating rises beyond its owner's authority and stays there, move ownership to someone who can accept and fund it; refer one-off decisions upward.

questions.subtopic: 3B3 Control testing methodologies. An earlier test after staff changes
questions.question: A shoe maker's ratings credit the planners' daily check of production orders against approved materials lists. It tested effective in January. Half the planners have since been replaced. What is the risk analyst's BEST next step?

options.A: Obtain the control owner's word that it still runs
options.B: Test a sample of checks the new planners have run
options.C: Review the training records of the planners who joined
options.D: Walk through the check's design again with a new planner

questions.key_concept: Earlier test results lose weight when conditions change; after turnover among the people running a control, test its operation since the change.
questions.pre_read: Notice what has changed since the control was last tested.
questions.correct_explanation: January's result was earned by the planners who ran the check then. With half of them replaced, the conditions behind that result have changed, so it no longer shows the check works today. Testing a sample of the checks the new planners have run gives current evidence of operation. Reviewing the new planners' training records is the runner-up: it shows they were taught the check, not that they perform it correctly.

wrong_explanations.A: A statement that the check still runs is inquiry, the weakest evidence on its own, and the owner may not see how new planners perform it.
wrong_explanations.C: Training records show the new planners were taught the check; they do not show it has been performed, or performed correctly, since they started.
wrong_explanations.D: Nothing in the check's design has changed; the people running it have, so a new walkthrough repeats a design test when operation is in question.

tips: Eliminate: A rests on the owner's word alone, the weakest evidence, and D retests a design that has not changed, when the people running it have.
Final two: B beats C because training records show what the new planners were taught; a sample of the checks they ran shows whether the control operates now.
Exam cue: an earlier test result holds only while the conditions behind it hold; after a material change, such as new people running a manual control, test the period since.

questions.subtopic: 3C5 Risk and control reporting techniques. A report that arrives after the budget
questions.question: An antique dealer's partners set spending each January. The risk analyst's yearly report, sent in April, has shown online fraud above appetite for two years. No treatment was funded. What is the analyst's BEST change?

options.A: Send the report before the partners set spending
options.B: Estimate treatment spending for the April report
options.C: Show the partners the fraud risk a band above its rating
options.D: Send the April report to the shop managers as well

questions.key_concept: Risk reporting is timed to the decisions it informs, such as budget setting, so that risk shapes choices instead of reviewing them afterward.
questions.pre_read: Compare when the report arrives with when the decision is made.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk report serves decisions, and the partners make their spending decision in January. A report arriving in April describes a risk the budget has already passed over, which is why two years of above-appetite ratings funded nothing. Sending the report before the partners set spending puts the risk in front of the decision. Estimating treatment spending for the April report is the runner-up: costs help a decision, but by April the money is allocated.

wrong_explanations.B: Treatment costs make a report more useful for deciding, but in April the year's spending is already set; better content arriving after the decision changes nothing.
wrong_explanations.C: Ratings are reported as assessed; inflating one to draw attention misleads the partners and undermines trust in every other rating in the report.
wrong_explanations.D: Shop managers cannot set the dealer's spending; adding readers without that authority does not bring the risk to the decision that funds treatment.

tips: Eliminate: C inflates a rating to draw attention, which misleads, and D adds readers who cannot set spending, so neither reaches the decision.
Final two: A beats B because the partners decide spending in January; cost estimates help only if they arrive while the money is still unallocated.
Exam cue: a risk report must reach decision makers before the decision it should inform, such as the budget round; content that arrives afterward describes a choice already made.

questions.subtopic: 3B2 Control design, selection, implementation and analysis. Travel claims within the limits
questions.question: A review found members' travel claims at a parliamentary office were within allowed amounts but covered private trips. The office handles about 400 claims a month. Which control should the risk analyst recommend as BEST?

options.A: A claims officer's check of trips against official agendas
options.B: Rules that flag claims above set amounts for review
options.C: Signed statements from members that their trips were official
options.D: Publication of members' names alongside their claim totals

questions.key_concept: A control should test the condition that failed, here a trip's purpose, against records the claimant does not keep, at a volume people can check.
questions.pre_read: Ask which condition the private trips broke and which control actually tests it.
questions.correct_explanation: The claims passed because nobody checked what the trips were for. A claims officer comparing trips with the office's official agendas tests that purpose against records the claimant does not keep, and at about 400 claims a month a person can do it. Signed statements from members are the runner-up: they may deter, but they ask the people who made the private claims to vouch for their own trips.

wrong_explanations.B: The private trips were within the allowed amounts, so a rule on amounts would pass them; it tests the condition that held, not the purpose that failed.
wrong_explanations.C: A signed statement relies on the members who made the private claims to judge their own trips; it may deter, but it adds no independent check of purpose.
wrong_explanations.D: Publishing names and totals shows how much members claim, not what the trips were for; claims within the allowed amounts would look normal.

tips: Eliminate: B tests amounts, which the private trips already met, and D publishes totals that say nothing about what a trip was for.
Final two: A beats C because a statement from the claimant is not an independent check; an officer comparing trips with official agendas tests purpose against records the claimant does not keep.
Exam cue: when a control passes items that meet its rule but fail its purpose, choose a check of that purpose against independent evidence, not the claimant's word.
